topic: Albert Bandura (1961): Stanford Nursery Bobo Doll Experiment & Observational Social Learning
visual_mode_reason: Bandura's nursery playroom sequence — adult striking an inflatable 5-foot Bobo doll with a wooden mallet and preschooler copying the exact verbal and physical script — is 100% behavioral staging.

primary_case.title: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross & Sheila Ross's Stanford Nursery Bobo Doll observational aggression study
primary_case.place: Stanford University Nursery School, Palo Alto, California

people.name: Albert Bandura
people.role: Stanford psychologist who proved complex novel behaviors are acquired by pure observation without direct reward

people.name: Dorothea Ross & Sheila A. Ross
people.role: Stanford co-investigators who staged the adult model scripts and scored blind one-way mirror behavior

people.name: 72 Stanford Nursery preschoolers (36 boys, 36 girls, ages 37-69 months)
people.role: Matched on baseline nursery aggression ratings across aggressive, non-aggressive, and control rooms

core_facts.fact: In 1961 at Stanford University Nursery School, Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, and Sheila Ross tested 72 children aged 3 to 5 years (mean age 52 months), pre-matched for baseline aggressiveness.

Children were assigned individually to one of three conditions: watching an adult attack a 5-foot inflatable Bobo doll for 10 minutes, watching an adult quietly assemble Tinkertoys for 10 minutes, or no adult model.

In the aggressive room, the adult followed a choreographed sequence: laying the Bobo doll on its side, sitting on it, striking its nose with a wooden mallet, tossing it in the air, and shouting unique phrases like 'Sock him in the nose!' and 'Pow!'

Next, every child underwent mild frustration calibration — briefly playing with attractive toys before being told those toys were 'reserved for other children' — and moved to a test room containing both peaceful toys and a 3-foot Bobo doll with a mallet.

Scored across 240 five-second intervals through a one-way mirror, children who watched the aggressive adult committed roughly twice as much imitative physical and verbal aggression as non-aggressive or control groups.
Children copied the adult's exact novel choreography word for word ('Sock him in the nose!') AND invented new non-imitative aggressive uses for other toys at higher rates.
Watching the calm Tinkertoy adult didn't merely leave children neutral — it actively suppressed subsequent aggression BELOW the no-model control baseline.

Boys exhibited more total physical aggression than girls overall (e.g., averaging 38.2 imitative physical acts after a male model vs 12.7 for girls after a male model), while verbal imitation rose sharply when model and child shared the same gender.
Zero stickers, candy, or praise were ever given to the children — demolishing radical behaviorism's claim that learning cannot occur without direct reinforcement.

In 1963, Bandura's team proved children imitated the exact same Bobo sequence just as strongly after watching it on a television screen, and in 1965 showed children still learned the script when the model was punished, waiting only for an incentive to perform it.

wow_facts.fact: Without receiving a single piece of candy, sticker, or word of praise, four-year-olds walked into the next room, picked up a wooden mallet, and shouted the adult's exact scripted phrases word for word.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Pure observation rewired behavior with zero direct reinforcement.

wow_facts.fact: Children who watched an adult quietly build Tinkertoys for ten minutes actually became calmer and LESS aggressive than children who saw no adult at all.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Calm role models are just as contagious as explosive ones.

wow_facts.fact: Two years later, Bandura played the exact same Bobo film on a television screen — and kids copied the filmed stranger almost identically.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Screens transmit behavioral scripts just as powerfully as live rooms.

wow_facts.fact: Even children who watched an adult get scolded for hitting Bobo could instantly demonstrate every single move the moment researchers offered juice for showing 'what the adult did'.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Punishment hides performance, not silent learning.

misconceptions.myth: Watching someone vent anger acts as 'catharsis' that drains away a viewer's own aggressive urges.
misconceptions.truth: Bandura's preschoolers showed the exact opposite: watching an aggressive model doubled aggressive acts rather than draining them.

misconceptions.myth: Learning only happens through trial-and-error rewards and punishments.
misconceptions.truth: Children acquired multi-step motor and verbal scripts purely by watching a 10-minute silent/spoken demonstration.

misconceptions.myth: Bobo doll hits prove every child became permanently violent toward peers.
misconceptions.truth: Critics rightly note weighted rebound dolls invite rough play and novel imitation, though follow-up studies confirmed cross-toy behavioral spillover.

misconceptions.myth: Only bad habits rub off through social modeling.
misconceptions.truth: The peaceful Tinkertoy model actively lowered aggression below control levels, proving self-regulation is socially modeled too.

everyday_hooks: Hearing your four-year-old repeat the exact frustrated phrase you muttered in traffic three days ago.
Watching a junior teammate adopt a manager's calm — or hostile — tone on client calls within two weeks of joining.
Picking up a friend's hand gestures and slang unconsciously after spending a weekend together.
Why 'do as I say, not as I do' loses every single time to visible adult actions.
